resources.string: Fire
In zero gravity a candle flame burns as a ball, not a teardrop: without gravity, hot air does not rise.
Water
Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold. It is called the Mpemba effect, and scientists still debate why.
Earth
A teaspoon of fertile soil holds more microorganisms than there are people on Earth.
Air
Air seems weightless, yet a cubic metre of it near the ground weighs about 1.2 kilograms.
Steam
True water vapour is invisible. The white cloud over a kettle is already tiny droplets cooling in the air.
Mud
Elephants and pigs wallow in mud on purpose: the crust protects their skin from sun and insects.
Dust
Dust from the Sahara crosses the Atlantic every year and fertilises the Amazon rainforest.
Lava
Basalt lava heats up to 1,200 °C — hotter than the melting point of copper.
Energy
Every second the Sun turns about four million tonnes of its own mass into energy.
Rain
Raindrops are shaped like burger buns, not teardrops: air resistance flattens them from below.
Stone
The Acasta Gneiss in Canada is about 4 billion years old, among the oldest known rocks of the Earth\'s crust.
Wind
The strongest gust measured outside a tornado, 408 km/h, was recorded in Australia during Cyclone Olivia in 1996.
Metal
Gallium is a metal that melts in your hand: it turns liquid at just 30 °C.
Sand
Much of the white sand on tropical beaches is made by parrotfish, which grind up coral.
Clay
Humanity\'s first written records, Sumerian cuneiform tablets, were made of clay.
Smoke
Smoke signals from watchtowers on the Great Wall warned of approaching enemies.
Ice
Ice is lighter than water, so lakes freeze from the top and fish survive the winter beneath it.
Cloud
A small cumulus cloud can hold hundreds of tonnes of water, kept aloft as tiny droplets by rising air.
Plant
Bamboo is the growth champion: some species add nearly a metre in a single day.
Ash
Volcanic ash is not soot but tiny shards of rock and glass, which is why it is so dangerous for aircraft.
Glass
The oldest glass beads were made in Mesopotamia about 4,500 years ago.
Lightning
A lightning channel briefly heats to about 30,000 °C — several times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Snow
Each snowflake is transparent, yet a snowdrift looks white: crystal faces scatter the whole spectrum of light.
Ocean
According to GEBCO in 2025, only 27.3% of the world\'s seafloor has been mapped in detail.
Mountain
The Himalayas are still rising: the Indian and Eurasian plates keep pushing them up by millimetres each year.
River
The Amazon carries about a fifth of all the river water that flows into the world\'s oceans.
Swamp
Peatlands cover only about 3% of the land but store roughly twice as much carbon as all the world\'s forests.
Tree
Methuselah, a pine in California, is about 4,800 years old — older than the pyramids of Giza.
Life
A human body holds roughly as many microbial cells as human ones.
Seed
A date palm was grown from a 2,000-year-old seed found at the Masada fortress.
Flower
Rafflesia arnoldii is the largest single flower: up to a metre across, and it smells of rotting meat.
Forest
The taiga is the largest land ecosystem: it stretches across Russia, Scandinavia, Canada and Alaska.
Moss
Mosses are among the oldest land plants: their ancestors reached land long before trees and dinosaurs.
Sky
The sky is blue because air scatters blue light more strongly. On Mars the sunsets are blue instead.
Sun
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
Moon
The Moon drifts away from Earth by about 3.8 centimetres every year.
Light
Light crosses the distance from Earth to the Moon in just over a second.
Shadow
The Moon\'s shadow races across Earth during a solar eclipse at over 1,700 km/h.
Time
Time runs slightly faster on a mountaintop than at its foot: atomic clocks notice it even over 30 cm.
Crystal
In Mexico\'s Cave of the Crystals, gypsum crystals grow longer than 10 metres.
Salt
Salt was once so valuable that its tax sparked revolts, such as the Salt Riot in Moscow in 1648.
Wave
The tallest wave ever officially measured and surfed was 26.21 metres, at Nazaré in Portugal.
Fish
Some fish can walk: mudskippers climb onto land and move on their fins.
Algae
About half of Earth\'s oxygen is made by ocean life, above all by phytoplankton.
Bird
The Arctic tern flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, up to 70,000 km.
Beast
The cheetah is the fastest land animal: over a short distance it can reach about 100 km/h.
Human
An adult usually has 206 bones, since many separate bones of a child\'s skeleton fuse with age.
Tool
The oldest known stone tools are about 3.3 million years old, older than the genus Homo itself.
Wood
Venice stands on wooden piles: waterlogged soil has almost no oxygen, so the wood decays very slowly.
House
In Çatalhöyük, one of the first towns, houses stood wall to wall with no streets, entered through the roof.
Field
In the Middle Ages a field was split in three and sown in turn to let the soil rest: the three-field system.
Farm
The first farms appeared about 11,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent of the Near East.
Wheat
More land on Earth is sown with wheat than with any other crop.
Bread
The oldest bread found is about 14,000 years old, baked before farming even began.
Cattle
A cow\'s stomach has four chambers, and microbes, mostly in the rumen, help it digest cellulose.
Milk
Most adults in the world digest milk sugar, lactose, poorly.
Cheese
The oldest cheese found is about 3,600 years old, discovered in graves in China\'s Taklamakan Desert.
Meat
Meat is red mostly because of the protein myoglobin, not because of blood left inside.
Leather
The oldest leather shoe found is about 5,500 years old, from the Areni-1 cave in Armenia.
Wool
A merino wool fibre is three to four times thinner than a human hair.
Cloth
China kept the secret of silk for thousands of years; smuggling out silkworm cocoons was said to be punishable by death.
Rope
The oldest known piece of rope is about 50,000 years old, twisted by Neanderthals.
Paper
Paper was made in China before our era; Cai Lun is credited around 105 CE with improving how it was made.
Ink
A cuttlefish squirts ink to confuse predators. Its ink once gave us the brown dye sepia.
Book
The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest known printed book with a precise date.
Knowledge
By ancient estimates the Library of Alexandria held tens or even hundreds of thousands of scrolls.
Wheel
The potter\'s wheel came before the wheeled cart: people spun clay first and only later built carts.
Cart
A wheel with an axle found in the Ljubljana Marsh in Slovenia is over 5,000 years old.
Road
The Roman road network ran for hundreds of thousands of kilometres, tens of thousands of them paved.
Village
The first permanent villages appeared before farming, where wild grains and game were plentiful.
Settlement
People lived in Jericho over 10,000 years ago, one of the oldest permanent settlements in the world.
City
Uruk in Mesopotamia is counted among the first cities: 5,000 years ago tens of thousands of people lived there.
Bridge
The Arkadiko Bridge in Greece was built over 3,000 years ago, and you can still walk across it.
Boat
The oldest boat found, the Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, is about 10,000 years old.
Sail
Egyptians sailed the Nile under sail more than 5,000 years ago.
Ship
The Titanic had 16 watertight compartments, but the iceberg damaged too many of them at once.
Port
Romans used concrete that could harden underwater to build long-lasting harbours and port structures.
Net
The oldest fishing net found is about 10,000 years old, discovered in Finland.
Fisherman
In China and Japan, fishermen caught fish with trained cormorants for centuries.
Feather
Birds\' feather counts vary widely: small ones may have thousands, large waterfowl tens of thousands.
Egg
An ostrich egg weighs as much as about two dozen hen\'s eggs, the largest of any living bird.
Nest
Weaver birds build nests from blades of grass and tie real knots with their beaks.
Bee
To make one kilogram of honey, a hive visits flowers millions of times, by some estimates.
Honey
Honey keeps unusually long thanks to little available water, a lot of sugar and an acidic environment.
Fruit
Botanically, a strawberry is not a berry, but a banana is.
Vegetable
Botanically a tomato is a berry, but in 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled it a vegetable.
Herbs
Mint feels cool without being cold: menthol activates the same skin receptors that sense cold.
Medicine
Fleming noticed that mould in a lab dish stopped bacteria growing — that is how penicillin was found.
Poison
Paracelsus is credited with the principle that the dose makes the poison: nearly anything is harmful in a large enough dose.
Mushroom
A honey fungus in Oregon covers nearly 10 km² and is one of the largest known organisms on Earth.
Bone
Bone is constantly rebuilt: special cells break down old bone while others build new bone.
Skull
A newborn\'s skull is made of movable plates with soft spots, so the head can grow.
Blood
One cubic millimetre of blood holds about 5 million red blood cells.
Corpse
Hair and nails do not grow after death: it is an illusion, as the skin dries and pulls back.
Ghost
In ancient Rome the Lemuria rite was held in May to drive restless spirits of the dead from the home.
Spirit
\"Spirit\" comes from Latin spiritus, \"breath\": alchemists called volatile substances spirits, hence strong liquor.
Cemetery
Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris is the resting place of Chopin, Molière and Édith Piaf.
Grave
The oldest known deliberate human burials are about 100,000 years old, found in caves in Israel.
Wolf
Domestic dogs descend from an ancient population of grey wolves; scientists still work out where and how.
Horse
Horses can doze standing up: a special leg structure locks the joints so the animal does not fall.
Rider
Couriers of the Mongol Yam postal system covered huge distances by changing horses at a network of stations.
String
A violin sounds when the bow rubs the string, and bows were made of horsehair for centuries.
Bow
Stone points from South Africa suggest bows and arrows may have been used tens of thousands of years ago.
Hunter
Humans are well suited to running long distances in heat: sweating carries away warmth during prolonged effort.
Arrow
Ötzi the Iceman, who lived 5,300 years ago, was killed by an arrow whose head was found in his shoulder.
Spear
The wooden Schöningen spears in Germany are about 200,000 years old, among the oldest surviving hunting weapons.
Sword
The pattern of Damascus blades came from the metal itself: high-carbon crucible wootz steel.
Shield
Roman legionaries formed a \"tortoise\" of shields, covered on every side and from above.
Armor
A full knight\'s armour weighed about 20–25 kg, and a knight could still run and vault into the saddle.
Warrior
The Terracotta Army has over 8,000 warriors, built from repeated parts, with faces and finish made individual.
Campfire
By various estimates, people have used fire for about a million years.
Tent
Bedouin tents were woven from goat hair: when wet, the fibres swell and the cloth sheds rain better.
Camp
Everest Base Camp sits at about 5,300 metres, higher than any peak in the Alps.
Forge
Smiths judged a metal\'s temperature by eye, by its glow: from dark red to bright yellow.
Hammer
In Norse myth, Thor\'s hammer Mjölnir always returned to the god\'s hand after being thrown.
Plow
The heavy plough let medieval farmers break the dense soils of northern Europe and feed more people.
Mine
The world\'s deepest mine, Mponeng in South Africa, reaches almost 4 kilometres underground.
Gold
Gold is so dense that a litre of pure gold weighs about 19.3 kilograms.
Silver
Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other metal.
Gem
Diamond and graphite are both carbon, but their atoms are bonded differently: one is clear and hard, the other soft and dark.
Crown
The Great Imperial Crown of Russia is set with almost five thousand diamonds.
King
Louis XIV ruled France for 72 years, longer than any other monarch in European history.
Queen
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
Castle
Windsor Castle is the oldest and largest inhabited castle in the world, a royal home for nearly a thousand years.
Tower
The Eiffel Tower was built as a temporary structure, meant to be taken down after 20 years.
Temple
Angkor Wat in Cambodia is the largest religious monument in the world.
Statue
The Statue of Liberty was originally copper-red and turned green as the copper oxidised in the air.
Garden
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon are the only one of the Seven Wonders whose existence was never proven.
Fountain
Coins tourists toss into Rome\'s Trevi Fountain are collected regularly and given to charity.
Park
Yellowstone, founded in 1872, became the world\'s first national park.
Market
Istanbul\'s Grand Bazaar is one of the oldest covered markets in the world, with about 4,000 shops.
Barrel
A barrel is bulged for a reason: such a heavy load is easy to roll and turn on the move.
Juice
To make one litre of maple syrup, about 40 litres of maple sap usually have to be boiled down.
Wine
The oldest traces of winemaking, about 8,000 years old, were found in clay vessels in Georgia.
Beer
Part of the pay for the builders of the Egyptian pyramids was given in beer.
Tavern
Ireland\'s Sean\'s Bar traces its history to a tavern on the same spot over a thousand years ago, as the tale goes.
Bakery
In Pompeii, bread was found that had lain under volcanic ash for almost 2,000 years.
Mill
The first windmills appeared in Persia over a thousand years ago, with sails turning horizontally.
Farmer
Farming arose independently in several parts of the world, including the Near East, China and Mesoamerica.
Baker
The word \"company\" literally means \"those who share bread\", from Latin com, \"with\", and panis, \"bread\".
Blacksmith
Smith, Schmidt, Kowalski and Kuznetsov are all surnames that mean the same thing: \"blacksmith\".
Miner
Miners took canaries underground: the bird felt dangerous gas first and warned the people.
Merchant
The Silk Road was not one road but a network of land and sea routes from China to the Mediterranean.
Scholar
Over 2,000 years ago Eratosthenes measured Earth\'s circumference using the shadow of a pole, and came very close.
Priest
Latin pontifex is usually read as \"bridge builder\": it was the name of the members of Rome\'s college of priests.
Sailor
Citrus fruit helped sailors prevent scurvy long before scientists identified vitamin C in the 20th century.
Captain
Magellan began the first voyage around the world but did not finish it: he died in the Philippines.
Pirate
\"Walking the plank\" was made famous by books and films; there is almost no solid evidence pirates did it.
Storm
About 2,000 thunderstorms are raging over Earth at any given moment.
Hurricane
Hurricane, typhoon and tropical cyclone are names for one kind of storm, used in different regions of the world.
Blizzard
An Antarctic blizzard is often not new snow: strong wind lifts and carries snow already lying on the surface.
Volcano
The largest volcano in the Solar System, Olympus Mons on Mars, is two and a half times taller than Everest.
Desert
The largest desert in the world is Antarctica: a desert is a place that gets almost no precipitation.
Oasis
Many Sahara oases are fed by groundwater stored thousands of years ago, when the desert was green.
Jungle
In a rainforest most nutrients are held in the plants themselves: heavy rain quickly washes them out of the soil.
Island
Greenland is the largest island in the world. Australia, which is bigger, is counted as a continent.
Beach
On some beaches and dunes the sand \"sings\": it hums or squeaks underfoot.
Coral
The Great Barrier Reef stretches about 2,300 kilometres and is made of almost 3,000 separate reefs.
Shark
Sharks are older than trees: they appeared more than 400 million years ago.
Mermaid
Sailors of the past mistook manatees for mermaids. Even Columbus wrote that he saw three \"sirens\".
Dragon
In China, fossil bones were sold for centuries as \"dragon bones\" and used in traditional medicine.
Phoenix
According to Herodotus, the phoenix flew to Heliopolis in Egypt once every 500 years to bury its father.
Griffin
One hypothesis holds that fossil finds in Central Asia fed the legends of griffins, though this is disputed.
Unicorn
Medieval \"unicorn horns\", sold for huge sums, were actually narwhal tusks.
Golem
Legend says Rabbi Loew of Prague shaped the Golem from clay to protect the Jewish quarter.
Magic
The word \"magic\" comes from \"magi\", the name of the priests of ancient Persia.
Wizard
\"Wizard\" comes from Middle English wys, \"wise\": a wizard was originally just a wise man.
Alchemy
The alchemists\' dream came true in the 20th century: physicists turned bismuth into gold, at a cost above the gold\'s worth.
Rune
The word \"rune\" meant \"secret\" in the ancient Germanic languages.
Potion
Ancient theriac was thought to cure everything: some recipes had about 60 ingredients, including opium and viper flesh.
Elixir
The word \"elixir\" comes from Arabic al-iksir, the alchemists\' name for a powder meant to transmute metals.
Portal
Relativity allows for \"wormholes\", but it is unknown whether such tunnels can exist in nature.
Spellbook
A large medieval manuscript took the hides of many animals, and the biggest ones hundreds.
Enchantment
The English word \"charm\" comes from Latin carmen, \"song\" or \"incantation\".
Clock
Optical atomic clocks are so precise that over the age of the Universe they would be off by less than a second.
Hourglass
On ships, time was kept with a sandglass, and the ship\'s bell was struck each time it was turned.
Star
Looking at stars, we see their past: light from the nearest takes years to arrive, from distant ones thousands or millions.
Observatory
Ulugh Beg\'s observatory in Samarkand measured the length of the year in the 15th century to within a minute.
Astronomer
In 1610 Galileo saw four moons of Jupiter through a telescope, still called the Galilean moons.
Philosopher\'s Stone
Isaac Newton wrote about a million words on alchemy and seriously searched for the philosopher\'s stone.
